summary:
Balak repeatedly asks Balaam to curse Israel. Balaam answers that he can pronounce only what God gives him to say. In Job, Eliphaz speaks of cursing a fool’s home.

Phinehas follows an Israelite man into a tent in the camp at Shittim. During the siege of Samaria even a quarter of a kab of dove dung fetches five pieces of silver. Deuteronomy lists the stomach beside the foreleg and cheeks as the priest’s share of an ox or sheep. Numbers uses a suffixed form for the part of the woman’s body pierced by Phinehas.

senses.definition: Call down harm on someone or something by speaking a curse.

evidence.note: Balak hopes that a curse will enable him to defeat Israel.
The renewed request comes with a promise of honour.
Balaam asks how he can curse a people whom God has not cursed.
Balak hears a blessing where he had commissioned a curse.
Balak takes Balaam to another viewpoint to repeat the attempt.
Balak asks Balaam to refrain from both cursing and blessing.
Balak hopes that God will allow a curse from a different place.
Balak says that Balaam has blessed his enemies three times.
Eliphaz says he cursed the dwelling of a fool who had taken root.

senses.definition: A tent or enclosed pavilion that a person can enter.

evidence.note: Phinehas enters after the Israelite and finds him with the Midianite woman inside.

senses.definition: A unit of capacity for dry goods. The price is quoted for a quarter of the unit.

evidence.note: The narrator gives two prices to convey the severity of the famine, one for a donkey’s head and one for a quarter-kab of dove dung.

senses.definition: The stomach portion set aside for the priest when an ox or sheep is slaughtered.

evidence.note: The instruction names the animal and assigns the priest three specific portions, ending with the stomach.

senses.definition: The part of the woman’s body through which the spear passes.

evidence.note: The feminine suffix identifies the woman as the person whose belly the spear reaches.

note:
The alternation between cursing and blessing in Numbers establishes the sense independently of an etymology. Its historical relation to נָקַב remains uncertain.

The Arabic and Mandaic words suggest a rounded roof. Numbers gives no description of its shape. The nearby word for the woman’s belly is a separate noun.

Merged from `qavav`, `qubbah` on 2026-11-20: one root, one entry.

Added 2026-11-21: קַב, from its former one-word entry. Filed under the geminate root קבב: Arabic قَبٌّ is 'a certain measure for corn', listed with قُبَّةٌ 'dome, vault' and قِبَّةُ الشَّاةِ 'a chamber of the sheep's stomach' under q-b-b (Lane p. 2478), so the hollow measure belongs with the vaulted tent קֻבָּה (Num 25:8) already in this entry. The meaning has no tie to cursing (קָבַב), which shares the spelling.

Its former note: The Idumaean receipts abbreviate the measure to q. An Aramaic letter from Egypt spells it qb in an instruction about making bread. The biblical price establishes the fraction sold but gives no conversion.

Added 2026-11-21: קֵבָה, from its former one-word entry. Filed under the geminate root קבב: Arabic قِبَّةُ الشَّاةِ 'a chamber of the stomach of a sheep or goat' is under q-b-b beside قُبَّةٌ 'vault, dome' (Lane p. 2478), so the stomach goes with the vaulted tent קֻבָּה that Num 25:8 sets beside קֳבָתָהּ. Shares this root with קַב (qab) in the same batch.

Its former note: The pastoral and legal comparisons support a stomach compartment in Deuteronomy. The verse gives no anatomical description that settles which compartment. In Numbers the opening קֻבָּה names the enclosure Phinehas enters, while קֳבָתָהּ marks where he wounds the woman. The precise organ is uncertain. Dolgopolsky §1904 tentatively compares the longer Akkadian form.
